Controls (1)
Pool is a game in which players use the white (cue) ball
to knock balls 1 through 15 into the pockets of the table.
There are three rule sets:
"Nine-ball," "Rotation," and "Eight-ball."
To shoot the cue ball use
To adjust your position and change the point
where the cue ball is struck use

Controls(2)
If you pocket a ball (or balls) you can take another shot.
It is considered a foul if you pocket the cue ball or if
the cue ball fails to hit any balls.
When there is a foul, the opposing player is free to take
a shot after placing the cue ball anywhere on the table.
Pool
Rules forNine-ball
Nine-ball uses balls 1 through 9.
Players must pocket the balls on the table in order,
starting with the lowest-numbered ball.
The player who pockets the 9 ball first is the winner.
All balls pocketed on a foul (except for the 9 ball)
remain pocketed, and the game continues.
Pool
RulesforRotation
Rotation uses balls 1 through 15.
Players must pocket the balls on the table in order,
starting with the lowest-numbered ball.
Pocketing a ball awards the player with the same number
of points as the ball's number.
The first player to exceed 61 points is the winner.
If all balls are expended without any player exceeding 61,
the balls are racked again and play continues from a break
shot.
Pool
Rules of Eight-ball (1)
Eight-ball uses balls 1 through 15.
Balls are divided into two groups: balls 1 through 7 are
"Low Balls" and balls 8 through 15 are "High Balls."
The first ball that is pocketed after the break shot
determines the group you will be targeting.
Pool
Rules of Eight-ball (2)
To win, you must pocket the 8 ball after pocketing all of
the balls in your group. You can pocket the balls in your
group in any order.

Pocketing the 8 ball before all of the balls in your

Trick Shots
Occasionally, there are circumstances where a ball can not
be sunk conventionally. In such cases, the following trick
shots are possible:
Combination Shot
· Carom Shot
· Kiss Shot
Pool
Combination Shot:
Say you would like to pocket ball A. Instead of striking
ball A directly with the cue ball, you hit ball B, which
in turn hits ball A. Pocketing a ball in this manner is
referred to as a Combination Shot.
B
Pool
Carom Shot:
Say you would like to pocket ball A. Instead of striking
ball A directly with the cue ball, you hit ball B first,
after which the cue ball rebounds and strikes ball A.
Pocketing a ball in this manner is
referred to as a Carom Shot.
A

Kiss Shot:
Say you would like to pocket ball A. You strike ball A
directly with the cue ball, after which it changes its
path by ricocheting off ball B. Pocketing a ball in this
manner is referred to as a Kiss Shot.
B
Pool
Rules of Four-ball (1)
Four-ball is played on a table without pockets,
known as a carom billiards table.
Four balls (two cue balls and two red balls) are used.
The player who goes first uses a white cue ball,
and the other player uses a yellow cue ball.
A point is scored by caroming on two or more object balls.
The opponent's cue ball is also considered an object ball.
No point is scored when object balls collide.
Pool
Rules of Four-ball (2)
A player who scores gets to shoot again. When no point
is scored, it becomes the other player's turn to shoot.
The first player to reach the designated score wins.
Anchor Spaces
The four corners of a carom billiards table have an
area known as an anchor space, outlined in red.
If there are two or more object balls in a single
anchor space, a foul results if more than one
remains after two shots.

pausepar_pause_en/picture/rule_chinchiro: Cee-lo
How to Play:Getting Started
Cee-lo is a four-player game played with three dice.
Three dice are rolled. In the event that two numbers
match, the third, non-matching number becomes the "point."
Players compete for the highest point.
Cee-lo
How toPlay:Points
A point's numerical value determines its strength.
6 is the strongest and 1 is the weakest. If you win with
points 1 through 6, the return is the same as your stake.
If you do not establish a point after three rolls, it is
counted as an automatic loss. If any of the dice fly
out of the bowl, it is counted as "missing the pot,"
whichisalsoanautomaticloss.
There are a number of additional combinations that hold
special values.
Cee-lo
How to Play: Special Combinations
Trips
Achieved by rolling three dice of the same number.
Trips consisting of numbers 2 through 6 triple your stake.
Trips of all 1's is called an "ace out" and quintuples
your stake.
Achieved with a combination of 4, 5, and 6. Doubles your
stake.
Achieved with a combination of 1, 2, and 3. However, the
combination results in a loss of double your stake.
Cee-lo
How to Play: Special Combinations
Musashi :
Rolling 6, 3, and 4 has the same value as getting a 6, but
doubles the amounts won or lost.
All-odds
Rolling 1, 3, and 5 counts the same as the previous player's
roll. Counts as a 3 when rolled by the first player or banker.
All-evens:
Rolling 2, 4, and 6 will count the same as the next player's
roll. Counts as a 4 when rolled by the first player or banker.

completed.
However, the outcome of the game is decided on the spot if
the banker rolls one of the combinations on the next page.

Omaha Hold 'em is a poker game in which you build
five-card hands from nine cards (two out of four
hole cards, plus three out of five community cards).
·HowtoWin:
- Have the strongest hand at the showdown.
All the other players fold.

GamePlay
In the first round, each player is dealt two hole cards.
Three community cards are dealt in the second round.
The fourth and fifth community cards are dealt in the third
and fourth rounds, respectively.

All players have placed bets of the same amount.
- The turn has been checked around.
At the end of the fourth round, all players reveal their hands
in a showdown. The player with the strongest hand wins.
